title: What is Microsoft Fabric API for GraphQL?
summary: Microsoft Learn's conceptual overview of Fabric's API for GraphQL: a no-code data access layer that auto-generates a GraphQL schema and endpoint over Fabric data sources so applications can query exactly the fields they need in one round trip, instead of teams hand-building REST services or wiring SQL drivers into every app.
audience: Application/integration developers building on Fabric data, data engineers who need to expose lakehouse/warehouse data without writing backend code, and architects scoping how external apps will consume Fabric items.
why_it_matters: GraphQL API is one of the newer, less-documented entry points into Fabric (AI & APIs section of the topic tree had no sources yet). Understanding what it can connect to and how schema evolution works is needed before recommending it as an integration pattern in any architecture.
takeaways: GraphQL API is a configuration-driven, no-backend-code way to expose Fabric Warehouse, SQL database, Lakehouse, and mirrored-database data to applications.
It is positioned as an alternative to both raw SQL-driver connections and hand-rolled REST APIs, removing the over-fetch/under-fetch and N+1 round-trip problems of each.
Schema changes are additive by default (no v1/v2/v3 endpoints), which simplifies client compatibility over time but shifts the burden onto disciplined field deprecation.
Coverage today is read/query-oriented for SQL Analytics Endpoint-backed sources, with mutation support tied to which data source type is attached.
The same overview page now points at an MCP (Model Context Protocol) tutorial, signaling Fabric's GraphQL endpoint is being positioned as an AI-agent data access surface, not just a human-facing API.

claims.text: Fabric API for GraphQL automatically generates a GraphQL schema, resolvers, and a live endpoint from connected data sources, so no custom backend code is required to expose the data.

The API for GraphQL is built so a single query can request only the specific fields a client needs and traverse defined relationships in one round trip, avoiding both over-fetching and the N+1 query pattern common to REST.

Supported data sources for the GraphQL API include Fabric Data Warehouse, Fabric SQL database, Fabric Lakehouse (via its SQL analytics endpoint), Azure SQL Database, and Fabric mirrored databases (including Azure SQL DB, Azure SQL Managed Instance, Cosmos DB, Fabric SQL Database, Azure Databricks, Snowflake, and open mirrored databases) accessed through their SQL analytics endpoints.

Setting up a GraphQL item in Fabric is a portal-driven workflow: create the item, connect data sources, choose which tables/views/stored procedures to expose, optionally model relationships, and configure access permissions, after which the endpoint is immediately queryable with no separate deployment step.
GraphQL items support fan-out queries across multiple attached data sources and can model one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many relationships between exposed entities.
Fabric's GraphQL schema evolution favors additive, non-breaking changes and field deprecation over issuing versioned endpoints (v1/v2/v3), since clients only receive fields they explicitly request.
The GraphQL API includes an interactive editor in the Fabric portal with a results pane, parameterized query/mutation support, and schema-aware Intellisense for building and testing queries.
Fabric exposes a built-in performance monitoring dashboard with request logging for GraphQL API items, intended to track API usage and behavior over time.

Microsoft now documents a path to connect AI agents to Fabric data through the GraphQL endpoint using the Model Context Protocol (MCP), positioning the API as an agent-facing data access layer in addition to a human application API.
